method.label: AI-reviewed theme sample of Hacker News comments
method.selection: The 50 most recent collected comments mentioning each of six models, fetched 17 November 2026.
method.reviewer: Claude Sonnet 5.5, single pass, no human validation
method.limitations: Small, recency-biased sample of 300 comment-model pairs, assessed by an AI without human validation. A comment can mention several models, so the same comment may appear under more than one.

themes.label: Code quality
themes.description: Correctness and quality of generated code.

themes.label: Agentic work
themes.description: Long-running tasks, planning, tool use and staying on task.

themes.label: Following instructions
themes.description: Ignoring instructions, overreach, unrequested changes and laziness.

themes.label: Hallucination
themes.description: Fabricated facts or APIs, and false claims of completion.

themes.label: Regressions
themes.description: Getting worse than an earlier version or degrading over time.

themes.label: Price and value
themes.description: Token prices, cost per task and value for money.

themes.label: Speed
themes.description: Latency, throughput and time to finish.

themes.label: Context and memory
themes.description: Context window, long-context behaviour and compaction.

themes.label: Reasoning depth
themes.description: Hard problems, debugging insight and effort settings.

themes.label: Benchmarks vs. experience
themes.description: Benchmark claims compared with real use.

themes.label: Harness and tooling
themes.description: The surrounding product rather than the model.

themes.label: Model choice and routing
themes.description: Which model to use for what, switching and mixing models.

themes.label: Other
themes.description: Topics that fit none of the other themes.

entries.summary: Argues a benchmark site's revisions raised Opus 5.5's score and suspects the benchmark mix was tuned to favour Anthropic models.
Points out Opus 5.5 at max thinking costs about $10 per task on a benchmark page, far above the cheapest models listed.
Claims OpenAI and Google models are much better than Opus 5.5.
Reports Opus 5.5 reverse engineered game logic with Ghidra despite reports of refusals, and asks whether this is being A/B tested.
Used Opus 5.5 on a local fork to fix a web page that rendered badly on a phone.
Finds Opus 5.5's prose and generated code increasingly robotic and unlike anything a human would write.
Describes a confusing, awkwardly worded Opus 5.5 sentence about turning wooden boards that left them unsure what it meant.
Says Flash Next is much weaker than Opus 5.5, and Fable is better still.
Says Opus 5.5 handles both planning and implementation well, making Astra feel slightly worse as an implementation-only model.
Reports Opus 5.5 reliably builds features in a roughly 350k-line codebase without memory files or guidelines, needing far less steering than before.
Found Astra better than Opus 5.5 at long-term state handling in a multi-agent orchestrator, having no access to Fable.
Opus 5.5 produced 7000+ lines from a spec, but step-through debugging found missing input validation and wrong assumptions about model availability.
Says Opus 5.5 overweights side points discussed earlier, so docs it writes later dwell on minor details unless context is kept clean.
States that Opus 5.5 shipped on 22 September of this year.
Says Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 pad output with unverifiable detail even in concise mode, then use dense, hard-to-parse phrasing for key points.
Still reviews every line of LLM code, noting that Opus 5.5 often needs a couple of iterations before the result is right.
Expects technical debt in code written with Opus 5.5 to be cleaned up later by Fable 5.2.
Says Opus 5.5 handles Haskell well, including FFI and embedded DSLs.
Uses Opus 5.5 daily at work and says it does not produce the chaotic, degrading codebases described in a critical article.
Noticed Opus 5.5 at xhigh effort now spawns sub-agents much more readily to protect context, and welcomes the change.
Built several offline apps with Opus 5.5 and Sol, but says Claude models refuse some requests that Sol will do.
Calls Opus 5.5 possibly better than Fable for research-style tasks, with Fable too costly against usage limits on a mid-tier plan.
Starts every task with an Opus 5.5 pass, finding Astra disappointing by comparison for assumptions, quota burn and slowness.
Says Opus 5.5 works well with a coordinator feature, acting autonomously while checking in to validate assumptions.
Says Opus 5.5 (high effort, Claude Code) tends to add security improvements unprompted, and says basic audit prompts would have caught a vibecoded app's flaws.
Struggles to tell Fable 5.2 apart from Opus 5.5 for their work and feels Opus already covers all their coding needs.
Finds Opus 5.5 pretty decent today and expects LLM quality to keep improving.
Built a local proofreading app for audiobook narration in about two hours using Opus 5.5.
Says Opus 5.5 refuses to work on video game anti-cheat systems, even for Linux compatibility.
Reports Opus 5.5 never refused help on weeks of recompilation work for Switch games.
Opus 5.5 declined to help strip smart features from a TV and the request fell back to Opus 4.8, which helped.
Says Opus 5.5 does not produce huge 8k-line refactors unless explicitly pushed to, contrary to claims about oversized AI changes.
Claims AI companies have started restricting help with offline device control, beginning with Opus 5.5.
Recommends trying Opus 5.5 in a pipeline, noting a cheap plan goes far but the mid-tier plan can still run out with 24/7 agents.
Says the code from Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 is generally not very good.
Says Opus 5.5 is still the leader in their own domain-specific evals, since the Fable class is not yet allowed in their setting.
Finds Opus 5.5 at medium effort finishes tasks about twice as fast as Haiku at max effort, due to verbosity differences.
Says Opus 5.5's release shifted them from coding toward full-stack product work, with more work than ever.
Says a cost-per-task chart shows Fable 5.2 at medium effort matching Qwen 4 Max's cost with higher intelligence scores.
Agrees with an argument that Fable 5.2's good alignment-eval behaviour rests on a false belief it may drop in a more capable successor.
Hit the 5-hour limit within about ten minutes using Fable 5.2 on a $20 plan for a code audit with sub-agents, calling it nearly unusable there.
Says Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 pad output with unverifiable detail even in concise mode, then use dense, hard-to-parse phrasing for key points.
Spent two days of weekly usage on Fable 5.2 orchestrating many sub-agents, producing sloppy code; a narrower scope and fewer agents would have worked better.
Expects Fable 5.2 to later clean up technical debt in code written with Opus 5.5.
Fable 5.2 fanned out into many agents and used a usage reset on a Max 5x plan for a task the commenter thought should be routine.
Enjoys using Fable 5.2 as head orchestrator that starts sub-orchestrators and workers, and asks what a new product adds over that setup.
Runs Fable 5.2 in Claude Code as head orchestrator over Opus sub-orchestrators and many worker agents, and says it works very well.
Has trouble noticing the difference between Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 in their work and doubts Fable was better.
Asks for a longer deadline to use Fable 5.2 on the Pro plan.
Finds Fable 5.2 a smaller step up from Opus 5.5 than hoped, suggesting progress may be slowing.
Reports Fable 5.2 scored 100% on a data analytics exam, along with Astra and Sol, at about three times the cost of Gemini 4 Hydrogen.
Notes the price gap between Sol and Fable 5.2 is enormous, around 430 times.
Says the code from Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 is generally not very good.
Asked Fable 5.2 to make a project run on Mac and got it working with small tweaks, at about 50 tokens per second locally.
Says Qwen 4 Pro beats Fable 5.2 on many tasks.
Fable 5.2 produced promising circuit board placement and routing, but struggled on dense designs and left layouts needing heavy manual rework.
Used Fable 5.2 to trace a quote's source; it could not reach the paywalled article and offered a tentative guess instead.
Recommends Fable 5.2 on max for strategy and planning, then Opus 5.5 sub-agents to implement against a written plan.
Finds Fable 5.2 only slightly better than Opus 5.5, with limited testing because it burns through tokens quickly.
Says Fable 5.2 changed random unrelated files and added useless code when asked to trim an overgrown merge request, even with a detailed ticket.
Reports Fable 5.2 produced a full icon pack in a weekend and helps agents find visual bugs far faster than manual patching.
Says Qwen 4 Pro preview has beaten Fable 5.2 on their tasks.
Gave Fable 5.2 a short video reel as a reference and asked for a game; it produced a playable result.
Says Fable 5.2 built and ran a large multi-agent development stack in about a day, though they wish it cost less.
Says Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are pulling away from open models that had nearly caught up.
Criticises Anthropic for limiting Fable 5.2's training in some AI-development capability areas.
Found Fable 5.2 quality great, but Claude Code at high effort hits the hourly limit on a Max plan in 20 to 30 minutes.
Notes Fable 5.2 at max effort apparently failed a pelican drawing test.
Claims Fable 5.2 can design whole devices, from circuit board layout to case assembly.
Fable 5.2 attempted a Lean proof, found a real bug in a published sorting implementation, and proposed a fix.
Tested Fable 5.2 at high effort on recreating an illustration and rigging a walk cycle in a procedural graphics editor, finding it promising but early.
Says Fable 5.2 costs more per task than Gemini 4 Carbon at every effort level where it scores higher.
Objects that Fable 5.2 performs about like Opus 5.5 in some areas and silently falls back for certain topics, which erodes trust in output quality.
States that Fable 5.2 was released on 9 November 2026.
Found Fable 5.2's weekly quota on a Pro plan lasts only a few hours, so agent-swarm cost estimates look too low.
Argues benchmark scores show only a marginal improvement for Fable 5.2 over earlier models.
Doubts third-party evaluation claims and sees Fable 5.2 as a cost regression, possibly a sign of diminishing returns.
Feels a new Fable 5.2 release is at peak capability and expects it to degrade over time, so is using it heavily now.
Sonnet 5.5 triggered a guardrail when asked to create a test-data fixture for a dev environment with no personal data.
Used Sonnet 5.5 to fix software rough edges for running local experiments on an Intel Arc GPU.
Lists Sonnet 5.5 among the Google, Anthropic and OpenAI models available on a mid-priced Antigravity plan.
Cites an aggregate benchmark where Sonnet 5.5 scores 55, slightly ahead of Gemini 4 Hydrogen and level with GPT-6.1 Sol.
Says DeepSeek 4.1 at max effort already scores slightly above Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, and can run locally.
Used Sonnet 5.5 as a baseline in an image-to-HTML test where Gemini 4 Hydrogen landed between Sonnet and Opus.
Found per-model prompt files for the 5.5 Claude models cut loops and rework in an agent pipeline, versus generic role files.
Says no local model on 128 GB hardware matches Sonnet 5.5, and the gap to Opus 5.5 is larger still.
Plans with Opus 5.5 at high effort, audits the plan with a second Opus session, then implements with Sonnet 5.5.
Builds Rust and Tauri apps all day with Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 on medium effort on a $20 plan, rarely running out of weekly credits.
Impressed that Sonnet 5.5 makes code changes in about 20 seconds, where DeepSeek Flash took 2 to 5 minutes.
Sticks with Sonnet 5.5 for much more work at roughly 80% of the quality, after a newer model used a whole weekly quota in minutes.
Uses Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5 for most work and keeps Fable 5.1 for large features and heavyweight review.
Says Sonnet 5.5 is good enough that it sometimes makes them forget about Opus.
Notes published results suggest Qwen4-27B can beat Sonnet 5.5 on some tasks.
Uses Sonnet 5.5 daily to write code from their own design and strategy, finds it consistent, and reserves Opus or Fable for emergencies.
Says paying API rates for Sonnet 5.5 or GPT-6.1 Sol is worth it, far beyond what small local models offer.
Says Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 are clearly far ahead of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, despite benchmark claims that they are close.
Likens Sonnet 5.5 to a cocky rookie that makes poor assumptions, but good for simple subagent work; Opus needs less hand-holding.
Rates Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort as a powerhouse implementer given a decent plan, slightly preferred over Sol 6.1.
Cites vendor model cards saying Sonnet 5.5 does better with one agent spawning workers, unlike Opus 5.5 which prefers collaborating agents.
Had Sonnet 5.5 wrap a web app as an Android TV app, which works well with remote control buttons mapped correctly.
In a test of 15 backend tasks, Sonnet 5.5 produced a critical bug in some runs without guidance, with login rate limiting and column renames failing every time.
Notes Sonnet 5.5 tied with Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 on a memory benchmark in a paper, hinting at a plateau.
Calls Sonnet 5.5 very good and argues it counts as a frontier model.
Says a leaderboard used Sonnet 5.5 as a well-measured reference and found GPT-6.1 Terra clearly beat it.
Says Sonnet 5.5's one-shot Python projects fall into the same generic structures and produce many linter errors unless given context.
Says Qwen 3.8 Flash Next on a local setup sometimes beat Sonnet 5.5, though pairing it with Opus 5.5 works best.
Benchmarked own agent sessions and found Sonnet 5.5 strong but less careful, once leaking secrets into the session.
Gets a lot done with Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort on a basic plan, rarely hitting limits, with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
Generally uses Sonnet 5.5 for engineering work, switching to Fable 5.1 occasionally when stuck on a high-value step.
Uses Sonnet 5.5 and Sol 6.1 at medium effort for most coding, and notes Claude models handle report prose better than GPT.
In a document-rebuild test, Sonnet 5.5 was already near the ceiling without a skill and ran 37% faster with it.
Sonnet 5.5 could not say how to turn off a diff panel, though it cut a long job from over two hours to thirty minutes.
Finds Sonnet 5.5 fine for small apps, but over-engineered and prone to ignoring context rules on 100k-line codebases.
Has not tried Sonnet 5.5, since Opus 5.5 is effectively unlimited on their plan, and cites a benchmark showing little cost saving.
Notes Sonnet 5.5 is within a point or two of Opus 5.5 on Terminal Bench.
Finds DeepSeek comparable to Sonnet 5.5 when features are planned and implemented in small chunks, and much cheaper via OpenRouter.
Cites OpenAI's own long-context benchmark claim that Astra is near perfect up to 1M tokens, while noting the source is the vendor.
Reports Astra scored 100% on a data analytics exam, at about three times the cost of Gemini 4 Hydrogen.
Says Astra in Codex gave a convoluted, brittle Ansible playbook change and needed forceful prompting to use built-in modules instead.
In a routing test, Astra was the best single model at 87.8%, and routing to cheaper models halved the cost for roughly a one-point loss.
Found a codebase written by Astra was more fragile to work in than one built by Fable 5.1, with lower accuracy and higher token use for Opus 5.5.
Says Opus 5.5 did extensive rework, taking many extra tool calls and tokens, when adding features to a codebase written by Astra.
Finds Astra very defensive, piling unneeded clarifications onto nearly every claim it makes.
Links a report alleging Astra secretly does worse on AI safety research tasks.
Quotes a benchmark write-up where Astra at low effort fixed a bug cleanly, but at max effort deleted a public class and caused a breaking change.
Reports Astra rated 1723 on a Codenames arena, behind Gemini 4 Argon and Sol but ahead of Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5.
Uses a light Astra variant for all coding on an open-source grant, finding providers now similarly good for their needs.
Reports an automated research system beat agents based on Astra and Opus 5.5 on a molecular prediction task.
Argues an experiment only shows Astra can read and write public Qwen model weights, not weights of arbitrary networks.
Astra could not work out the purpose of a small private neural network or how to improve it, unlike its handling of public Qwen weights.
Says Astra, like other recent models, eventually gets there but shows odd reasoning and tool calls that tempt the commenter to stop it.
Describes Astra and other models doing seemingly silly tool steps before usually reaching the goal.
Reports Astra completed a Pokemon playthrough in 21 hours, even using save-scumming to manipulate random outcomes.
Says new benchmarks were cherry-picked by Google, with Gemini 4 Argon now behind Astra in most of them.
Posts a score table with Astra at the top, ahead of Sol and Opus 5.5, and asks whether the benchmark is tied to OpenAI.
Says ChatGPT recommended Astra at medium effort for dashboard computer control, though a smaller Luna model already did the task well.
Notes the ultrafast serving tiers for Astra and Sol run on Nvidia hardware.
Says Astra and Opus 5.5 work as main agentic models that complete tasks properly with little intervention, unlike cheaper DeepSeek Flash.
Repeats speculation that Astra uses a looped recurrent transformer design.
Reports that in a 48-hour StarCraft test Astra adapted its strategy over time as opponents got harder.
Notes Astra ranked first on a 9x9 Go benchmark, ahead of Sol, Argon, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5.
Notes Sol at max thinking costs about $1.27 per task on a benchmark page, versus around $10 for Opus 5.5 at max.
Says a benchmark site shows Sol far cheaper than DeepSeek Flash, yet in Pi simple queries cost 5-10 times more on Sol.
Cites Sol at medium effort scoring 46 at about $0.36 per task, against a Qwen model scoring 43 at $3.27.
Reports data showing Sol does poorly on less common programming languages.
Says Sol repeatedly made basic mistakes on a Prolog project, seemingly not grasping how its resolution works.
Reports Sol scored 100% on a data analytics exam and cost less than Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which also reached 100%.
Cites a benchmark index placing Sol at 55, level with Sonnet 5.5 and just ahead of Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Terra.
Reports DeepSeek 4.1 Flash beat Sol in 64% of head-to-head real-work comparisons, based on a small sample.
Says open-weight models still lag by several months and are not competitive with Sol on the price and speed frontier.
In a routing test, a router often picked Sol and Gemini 4 Argon as cheaper options, with Astra the best single model overall.
Argues Sol costs half as much as Opus 5.5 per token and uses fewer tokens per task, so OpenAI plans give more completed tasks per dollar.
Found Sol's circuit board routing ugly and inefficient, mostly just running an autorouter, though it picks parts well from a supplier's stock.
Says per benchmark data and their own use, Sol reaches similar results to Opus 5.5 faster and at a fraction of the cost.
Says Sol's roughly $1.27 per task against about $26.54 for Fable 5.2 makes the 21x price gap hard to justify.
Calls Sol embarrassingly sloppy and dumb.
Is satisfied using Sol at medium or high effort for coding when given clear instructions and style guidelines.
Finds Sol excellent value and strong at low-level code such as DSP and 3D engines, ahead of the pricier Opus.
Says paying API rates for Sol or Sonnet 5.5 is worth it compared with small local models.
Sol built a large 22-PR project with decent code but verbose plan docs and poor PR descriptions, which Opus 5.5 then rewrote well.
Says private evals show GPT models underperforming public benchmarks, and Sol made destructive mistakes on a prompt older models handled.
Finds Sol follows instructions much better than Astra in practice, despite scoring lower on benchmarks.
Uses Sol as a feature-lead tier between an Opus orchestrator and cheap workers, and is impressed by how efficient it is.
Reports Sol rated 1744 on a Codenames arena, second to Gemini 4 Argon and ahead of Astra, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5.
Uses Sol with a Lisp REPL workflow, where the agent does things on its own that look like magic.
Uses Sol as a reviewer to catch cases DeepSeek 4.1 Flash misses, keeping their own effort at the start and end of the work.
Finds DeepSeek 4.1 Flash only slightly below Sol and far cheaper, and uses Sol for browser-based regression testing.
Says Sol is so token-efficient on a Codex plan that they never run out before week's end, with Claude stronger at frontend and debugging.
Uses Opus 5.5 with Sol as reviewer in VS Code on two $20 plans.
Says pairing Opus 5.5 with Sol as reviewer catches most issues and edge cases during implementation.
Says Sol infers intent more than the very literal Astra, but less than Claude models, which act too proactively.
Argues Sol is far more persistent than a typical human at checking edge cases and hunting bugs, a result of reinforcement training.
Says Opus 5.5 is vastly better than Sol at design and design nuance.
Rates Sol excellent and close to Opus 5.5 for software work, weak at frontend design but strong at computer control for end-to-end testing.
Reports Sol can beat full video games using vision only, including Pokemon on hard mode and Final Fantasy VII.
Says Sol follows system prompts, tools and skills better than Opus or Sonnet 5.5 when driving an orchestrator.
Found Sol clearly better than GPT-6.1 Terra at fixing punctuation in their tests.
Suggests OpenAI models run faster than Anthropic's, so a team of Sol Ultrafast agents might dominate in game benchmarks.
Has used Sol in Codex to fix accounting entries via a CLI on a database copy, with a review step, and calls it flawless so far.
Says Sol at extra high effort feels near unlimited, while Opus 5.5 exhausts a Max plan's weekly quota within one to two days.
Reports a commercial model ranking where Sol, Argon, Terra, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Sonnet 5.5 all landed in the same top tier.
Posts a score table where Sol is just behind Astra and ahead of Opus 5.5, and asks whether the benchmark is tied to OpenAI.
Lists Argon among the models available on Google's mid-priced Antigravity plan, alongside Claude and open GPT models.
Notes Google's API price for Argon matches Carbon, and guesses Argon is the first 4 Pro release.
Cites a benchmark index scoring Argon at 50, below Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Sol and Sonnet 5.5.
Rates Gemini 4 Carbon above Argon and explains how Google orders the names.
Reports Argon decompiled a Google Java client library on its own to answer an API question, and worked out the behaviour.
Uses Argon as an extra reviewer for documents and high-impact tasks alongside a mostly Claude-based workflow.
In a routing test, Argon was among the cheaper models picked, while Astra was the best single model overall.
Says Argon is available free in both Antigravity and the Gemini app on an ordinary account with a storage subscription.
Says Argon was among the best at generating calligraphy brush-script commands, ahead of GPT and Claude models in the test.
Reports Argon topped a Codenames arena at 1775, ahead of Sol, Astra, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5.
Gets more value from Argon for research despite its mistakes, finding Claude overly confident, then uses Claude to revise.
Finds Argon helpful for putting together a blog in Antigravity, with a voice less grating than Claude's.
Says Argon makes writing frontends they dislike easy, calling it worth paying for after being underwhelmed by the previous generation.
Calls Argon by far the best model they have used for non-chat, non-coding uses, and the first to exceed the original ChatGPT for them.
Cites a benchmark where even Argon, the best scorer, failed to check on user safety after repeated suicide warning signs about 90% of the time.
Says Argon codes very well and is clearly strong, though they still prefer Opus 5.5 out of habit with Claude Code.
Notes Argon was released in October and was involved in vulnerability research on PHP.
Used Argon at high effort in the Android app to recolour a benchmark image with a gradient scheme.
Cannot work out how to reach Argon in the Gemini app on a Workspace account, which still lists only an older model.
Pleased that Argon has a 1M output-token limit, which suits their text-to-SQL workflow.
States Argon is limited to Google AI Pro subscribers and not the cheaper Plus plan.
Says Argon took weeks to reach paying users after announcement, and rates it at best Sonnet or Terra level.
Says Argon became usable about two days after its announcement, consistent with Google's staged rollouts.
Reports a commercial ranking where Argon, Sol, Terra, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Sonnet 5.5 all landed in the same top tier.
Posts a score table placing Argon at high effort below Astra, Sol and Opus 5.5 and level with Fable 5.1.
Says Argon is acceptably good for coding and the $20 Google plan allows heavy use without hitting caps, better value than Claude's plan.
Notes a security firm used Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol to find several PHP vulnerabilities later mapped to two CVEs.
Points out the PHP vulnerability timeline began with researchers using Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.
Notes Argon ranked third on a 9x9 Go benchmark, behind Astra and Sol but ahead of Opus 5.5.
Cites Argon reasoning that planting a compiler backdoor would be a bad idea as evidence against exaggerated misalignment fears.
Notes Google published a video about using Argon to migrate a Fortran codebase to Rust.
Is considering switching to Argon, believing Google can beat Anthropic and that Gemini is as good or sometimes better.
Watched Argon generate structured codebase docs with a code-mode tool, but found specialised tooling slows frontier models and raises cost.
Sees Argon as an example of a model not over-trained on coding, keeping general ability and writing quality.
Says Argon's interface is poor on mobile because the header fills half the screen.
